title: Ὁ λόχος καὶ ἡ χλαῖνα
titleEn: The Ambush and the Cloak — Odyssey 14.418–533
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The swineherd Eumaeus has a fat five-year-old pig killed for his guest. He burns hairs from its head as a first offering and prays for Odysseus's return, cuts up the meat, sets one share aside for Hermes and the nymphs, and honours the guest with the long cuts of the back. Odysseus, whom Eumaeus does not recognise, wishes him the love of Zeus, and Eumaeus answers that a god gives or withholds as he wills. After supper a bitter, rainy night comes on, and Odysseus, to test whether Eumaeus will lend him a cloak, tells a story of a freezing ambush before Troy: he had left his cloak behind and was freezing, until Odysseus spoke of a dream and Thoas ran off to the ships on that errand, leaving his cloak behind him. Eumaeus takes the hint. He promises the stranger a cloak for the night and clothes from Odysseus's son, makes a bed by the fire and covers him with a thick cloak of his own, and then arms himself and goes out to sleep beside his pigs under a rock.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας κέασε ξύλα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ,
οἱ δ’ ὗν εἰσῆγον μάλα πίονα πενταέτηρον.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas kease xyla nēleï chalkōi,
hoi d’ hyn eisēgon mala piona pentaetēron.
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he split wood with the pitiless bronze,
and they led in a pig, very fat, five-year-old.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and split wood with the pitiless bronze, and they led in a very fat pig, five years old.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας 'so then having spoken' is a stock opening: the actor has just finished speaking and now acts. The subject is not named; the next lines show it is the swineherd. κέασε is the unaugmented aorist of κεάζω 'split', and ξύλα, neuter plural, is wood for the fire. νηλέϊ is the dative of νηλεής 'pitiless', here of the bronze axe. οἱ δ’ is 'and they', a new subject the lines do not name, probably the other herdsmen (compare the ἑταῖροι of 462). εἰσῆγον is the imperfect of εἰσάγω 'lead in'. ὗν is the accusative of ὗς 'pig' and does not say whether it is male or female.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἔστησαν ἐπ’ ἐσχάρῃ·
sentences.tr: ton men epeit’ estēsan ep’ escharēi·
sentences.l: Him then they stood at the hearth;
sentences.i: Then they stood the pig at the hearth;
sentences.n: ἔστησαν is the aorist of ἵστημι used transitively: 'they stood (it) up', not 'they stood'. τόν is the pronoun 'him', the pig. ἐσχάρη is the hearth, the fire-place; ἐπ’ is ἐπί with the dative, 'at, by', and the pig is brought to the fire to be killed, not set on it. μέν looks ahead to οὐδὲ συβώτης in the next unit: the men do this, and the swineherd, for his part, does more.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ συβώτης
λήθετ’ ἄρ’ ἀθανάτων·
sentences.tr:
oude sybōtēs
lēthet’ ar’ athanatōn·
sentences.l:
and not the swineherd
forgot, then, the immortals;
sentences.i: and the swineherd did not forget the immortals;
sentences.n: λήθετ’ is a past tense of λήθομαι (Attic λανθάνομαι) 'forget', without augment; it takes the genitive, here ἀθανάτων 'the immortals', the gods. οὐδέ is 'and ... not'. ἄρ’ is the particle ἄρα, 'then, as one would expect'. The swineherd is not content to kill the pig: he also remembers the gods before the meat is shared.

sentences.t: φρεσὶ γὰρ κέχρητ’ ἀγαθῇσιν·
sentences.tr: phresi gar kechrēt’ agathēisin·
sentences.l: for with wits good he was provided;
sentences.i: for he was furnished with good wits;
sentences.n: κέχρητ’ looks like an elided κέχρητο, from χράομαι 'use, have the use of', here with a dative: 'he was furnished with'. The exact form is not certain, but the sense is plain from the line. φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν, and φρένες, the seat of understanding, are 'wits'. ἀγαθῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν (Attic -αῖς). γάρ gives the reason for the previous unit: this is why he did not forget the gods.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅγ’ ἀπαρχόμενος κεφαλῆς τρίχας ἐν πυρὶ βάλλεν
ἀργιόδοντος ὑός, καὶ ἐπεύχετο πᾶσι θεοῖσιν
νοστῆσαι Ὀδυσῆα πολύφρονα ὅνδε δόμονδε.
sentences.tr:
all’ hog’ aparchomenos kephalēs trichas en pyri ballen
argiodontos hyos, kai epeucheto pasi theoisin
nostēsai Odysēa polyphrona honde domonde.
sentences.l:
But he, making-the-first-offering, hairs of the head in the fire cast
of the white-toothed pig, and prayed to all the gods
that Odysseus the much-minded return home to his own house.
sentences.i: But he made the first offering, throwing hairs from the head of the white-toothed pig into the fire, and prayed to all the gods that Odysseus of the many counsels should return to his own home.
sentences.n: ἀπαρχόμενος is the participle of ἀπάρχομαι 'make a first offering'; the offering is the hairs cut from the pig's head, thrown on the fire (βάλλεν is an unaugmented imperfect). ἀργιόδοντος 'white-toothed' (ἀργι- 'white, bright' + ὀδούς 'tooth') is the genitive of an epithet of the pig, ὑός being its noun; the white teeth are its tusks. ἐπεύχετο takes the dative πᾶσι θεοῖσιν 'to all the gods' and an infinitive for the prayer: νοστῆσαι 'to return home'. ὅνδε δόμονδε is 'to his own house': ὅν is the possessive ὅς 'his own', and both words carry the suffix -δε 'toward'. Line 424 is word for word 1.83.

sentences.t: κόψε δ’ ἀνασχόμενος σχίζῃ δρυός, ἣν λίπε κείων·
sentences.tr: kopse d’ anaschomenos schizēi dryos, hēn lipe keiōn·
sentences.l: And he struck, raising himself, with a billet of oak, which he left, splitting;
sentences.i: and rising to the blow he struck with a billet of oak, one he had left over when he split the wood;
sentences.n: κόψε is the unaugmented aorist of κόπτω 'strike'. ἀνασχόμενος, 'raising himself (for the blow)', is the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω; the object, the pig, is not stated. σχίζῃ is the dative of σχίζα 'a split piece of wood, a billet', δρυός 'of oak'. ἣν is the relative 'which' (accusative), not the possessive. κείων is taken as 'splitting', a participle from the root of κεάζω, the verb of 418: the billet he left over from splitting the wood. It is a different word from the κείων of 532.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἔλιπε ψυχή.
sentences.tr: ton d’ elipe psychē.
sentences.l: And him the soul left.
sentences.i: and the soul left it.
sentences.n: ἔλιπε, with its augment, is the aorist of λείπω 'leave'; compare the unaugmented λίπε in the line before. τόν is the pronoun 'him', the pig. The stroke has killed it: its ψυχή, the 'soul', the breath of life, leaves the body. The sentence ends in the middle of line 426, and the next unit begins there.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἔσφαξάν τε καὶ εὗσαν·
sentences.tr: toi d’ esphaxan te kai heusan·
sentences.l: and they both slaughtered and singed;
sentences.i: then they slaughtered it and singed it;
sentences.n: τοί is the old form of the pronoun οἱ, 'they': the herdsmen. ἔσφαξαν is the aorist of σφάζω 'cut the throat of, slaughter'; εὗσαν is the aorist of εὕω 'singe', the bristles being burnt off before the carcase is cut up. τε καὶ is 'both ... and'. Neither verb has an object; it is understood, the pig.

sentences.t: αἶψα δέ μιν διέχευαν·
sentences.tr: aipsa de min diecheuan·
sentences.l: and quickly it they cut up;
sentences.i: and they quickly cut it up;
sentences.n: αἶψα 'quickly'; μιν 'him, it', the pig. διέχευαν is the aorist of διαχέω, literally 'pour apart', which gives 'cut up, divide'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ὠμοθετεῖτο συβώτης,
πάντων ἀρχόμενος μελέων, ἐς πίονα δημόν,
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν πυρὶ βάλλε, παλύνας ἀλφίτου ἀκτῇ,
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ōmotheteito sybōtēs,
pantōn archomenos meleōn, es piona dēmon,
kai ta men en pyri balle, palynas alphitou aktēi,
sentences.l:
and he laid raw pieces, the swineherd,
of all the limbs beginning, into rich fat,
and these in the fire cast, having sprinkled them with barley-meal’s grist,
sentences.i: and the swineherd, beginning with all the limbs, laid raw pieces in rich fat, and these he threw into the fire, sprinkled with barley-meal,
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is 'and he', with συβώτης added to say who. ὠμοθετεῖτο is the imperfect middle of ὠμοθετέω 'lay raw pieces of meat', from ὠμός 'raw' and the root of τίθημι. πάντων ἀρχόμενος μελέων 'beginning with all the limbs' means a piece is taken from each limb; ἐς πίονα δημόν 'into rich fat' means they are laid in fat; πίονα, 'fat', was μάλα πίονα of the pig at 419. τά μέν 'these' looks ahead to τἆλλα 'the rest' in the next unit. παλύνας is the aorist participle of παλύνω 'sprinkle'; ἀκτῇ is a rare word for ground grain, 'meal, grist', so ἀλφίτου ἀκτῇ is barley-meal. The sentence would run past four lines, so it is cut here at the comma.

sentences.t:
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρα τἆλλα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειραν,
ὤπτησάν τε περιφραδέως ἐρύσαντό τε πάντα,
βάλλον δ’ εἰν ἐλεοῖσιν ἀολλέα·
sentences.tr:
mistyllon t’ ara talla kai amph’ obeloisin epeiran,
ōptēsan te periphradeōs erysanto te panta,
ballon d’ ein eleoisin aollea·
sentences.i: they cut up the rest into small pieces, pierced them on spits, roasted them with great care, drew them all off, and threw them together on the boards;
sentences.n: μίστυλλον, ἔπειραν, ὤπτησαν, ἐρύσαντο and βάλλον are plural past tenses with no stated subject: the herdsmen. μιστύλλω is 'cut into small pieces', πείρω 'pierce, run through', ὀπτάω 'roast'; ἐρύσαντο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω 'draw', here 'draw off the spits'. περιφραδέως is 'very carefully' (περι- strengthens). ἐλεοῖσιν is a word for some board or table on which meat was set; its exact object is not known. ἀολλέα 'all together' is neuter plural. Line 430 is also 3.462.

sentences.t:
ἂν δὲ συβώτης
ἵστατο δαιτρεύσων·
sentences.tr:
an de sybōtēs
histato daitreusōn·
sentences.l:
and up the swineherd
stood, to carve;
sentences.i: and the swineherd stood up to carve the meat;
sentences.n: ἂν is ἀνά with its last vowel dropped, in tmesis with ἵστατο: ἂν δὲ ... ἵστατο is ἀνίστατο 'stood up'; ἵστατο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι. δαιτρεύσων is the future participle of δαιτρεύω 'carve, portion out', expressing purpose. The meat is roasted and heaped on the boards, and now the swineherd rises to share it out.

sentences.t: περὶ γὰρ φρεσὶν αἴσιμα ᾔδη.
sentences.tr: peri gar phresin aisima ēidē.
sentences.l: for exceedingly in his wits things in due measure he knew.
sentences.i: for in his wits he knew exceedingly well what was due.
sentences.n: περὶ ... ᾔδη is tmesis for περιῄδη: περίοιδα 'know exceedingly well'. ᾔδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα, used as a past 'knew'. αἴσιμα, neuter plural from αἶσα 'portion, due share', is 'things in due measure', things that are fair; φρεσίν is 'in his wits'. The line gives the reason the swineherd himself does the carving: he knows what is a fair share.

sentences.t: καὶ τὰ μὲν ἕπταχα πάντα διεμοιρᾶτο δαΐζων·
sentences.tr: kai ta men heptacha panta diemoirato daïzōn·
sentences.l: and these into seven parts all he divided, cutting up;
sentences.i: He divided it all into seven portions, cutting it up;
sentences.n: τά μέν is 'these', the roast meat. ἕπταχα 'in seven parts' is an adverb, and πάντα 'all of it'. διεμοιρᾶτο is the imperfect middle of διαμοιράομαι 'divide into shares', from μοῖρα 'portion', and δαΐζων 'cutting up' is a participle of δαΐζω. The next two lines say where the portions go.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν ἴαν νύμφῃσι καὶ Ἑρμῇ, Μαιάδος υἱεῖ,
θῆκεν ἐπευξάμενος, τὰς δ’ ἄλλας νεῖμεν ἑκάστῳ·
sentences.tr:
tēn men ian nymphēisi kai Hermēi, Maiados huiei,
thēken epeuxamenos, tas d’ allas neimen hekastōi·
sentences.l:
The one portion to the nymphs and to Hermes, Maia’s son,
he set down, praying, and the others he distributed to each;
sentences.i: One portion he set down for the nymphs and for Hermes, the son of Maia, with a prayer, and the others he distributed to each;
sentences.n: ἴαν is the Homeric feminine 'one' (Attic μίαν): 'the one portion', set apart for the gods. νύμφῃσι and Ἑρμῇ are datives; Μαιάδος υἱεῖ 'son of Maia' says which Hermes. The nymphs of the countryside and Hermes are gods a herdsman would honour. θῆκεν 'put down' goes with ἐπευξάμενος 'praying'. νεῖμεν is the aorist of νέμω 'distribute', unaugmented, with a movable ν; ἑκάστῳ is 'to each'. τὴν μέν ... τὰς δέ 'the one ... but the others'.

sentences.t:
νώτοισιν δ’ Ὀδυσῆα διηνεκέεσσι γέραιρεν
ἀργιόδοντος ὑός, κύδαινε δὲ θυμὸν ἄνακτος·
sentences.tr:
nōtoisin d’ Odysēa diēnekeessi gerairen
argiodontos hyos, kydaine de thymon anaktos·
sentences.l:
With chines, unbroken, Odysseus he honoured
of the white-toothed pig, and he exalted the heart of his lord;
sentences.i: He honoured Odysseus with long unbroken cuts of chine from the white-toothed pig, and so gladdened the heart of his lord;
sentences.n: νώτοισι is the dative plural of νῶτον 'back', here the chine, a cut from the pig's back; διηνεκέεσσι 'unbroken', that is in whole lengths, is a dative plural in -εσσι. γέραιρεν, imperfect of γεραίρω 'honour', is unaugmented; a long cut is the portion of honour. κύδαινε is from κῦδος 'glory': 'exalt', and so 'cheer'; θυμόν is 'heart'. ἄνακτος 'of his lord' is the narrator's word: within the scene Eumaeus treats the guest as a stranger (see 443 and 508), so he does not know whose heart he is cheering. Ὀδυσῆα is spelled with one σ here and with two at 447.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσας προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: kai min phōnēsas prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: And him, having spoken, addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: And Odysseus of many wiles spoke up and said to him:
sentences.n: καί μιν φωνήσας προσέφη is a speech introduction: φωνήσας 'having spoken out' with προσέφη 'addressed' together mean 'spoke up to him'. μιν is 'him', Eumaeus. πολύμητις 'of many wiles' is from μῆτις 'cunning intelligence'. The speech follows in the next line; the Greek has no quotation marks, and the English adds them.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ οὕτως, Εὔμαιε, φίλος Διὶ πατρὶ γένοιο
ὡς ἐμοί, ὅττι τε τοῖον ἐόντ’ ἀγαθοῖσι γεραίρεις.
sentences.tr:
aith’ houtōs, Eumaie, philos Dii patri genoio
hōs emoi, hotti te toion eont’ agathoisi geraireis.
sentences.l:
“Would that thus, Eumaeus, dear to Father Zeus you might become
as to me, because me, being such, with good things you honour.”
sentences.i: “If only, Eumaeus, you might become as dear to Father Zeus as you are to me, since, such as I am, you honour me with good things.”
sentences.n: αἴθε with the optative γένοιο (aorist of γίγνομαι) is a wish, 'would that you might become'; ὡς ἐμοί supplies 'as (dear) to me'. φίλος Διὶ πατρί: Διί is the dative of Ζεύς. ὅττι is ὅτι 'because', with the τ doubled for the verse. τοῖον ἐόντα 'being such' is accusative and refers to Odysseus himself, such as he is, and is the object of γεραίρεις 'you honour', which picks up γέραιρεν of 437. ἀγαθοῖσι is neuter, 'with good things'. Odysseus is speaking to his host without being known to him.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: προσέφης is the second person: the poet breaks off and speaks to Eumaeus, 'you addressed', and does so again at 507; the verb is πρός + the imperfect of φημί. τὸν is the pronoun 'him', Odysseus. ἀπαμειβόμενος 'answering' is the present participle of ἀπαμείβομαι. Εὔμαιε and συβῶτα are vocatives: συβῶτα has the Homeric vocative ending -α, as ἱππότα does.

sentences.t:
ἔσθιε, δαιμόνιε ξείνων, καὶ τέρπεο τοῖσδε,
οἷα πάρεστι·
sentences.tr:
esthie, daimonie xeinōn, kai terpeo toisde,
hoia paresti·
sentences.l:
“Eat, strange man among strangers, and take delight in these things,
such as are at hand;
sentences.i: “Eat, strange man among strangers, and enjoy these things, such as are at hand;
sentences.n: δαιμόνιε is the vocative of δαιμόνιος, an address whose force is uncertain: 'strange one', a man moved by something beyond himself; it can be gentle or reproachful. ξείνων is a partitive genitive, 'among strangers'. ἔσθιε and τέρπεο are imperatives, τέρπεο middle, 'enjoy yourself', with the dative τοῖσδε 'these things'. οἷα is 'such as', and πάρεστι 'is present, is at hand'.

sentences.t:
θεὸς δὲ τὸ μὲν δώσει, τὸ δ’ ἐάσει,
ὅττι κεν ᾧ θυμῷ ἐθέλῃ· δύναται γὰρ ἅπαντα.
sentences.tr:
theos de to men dōsei, to d’ easei,
hotti ken hōi thymōi ethelēi· dynatai gar hapanta.
sentences.l:
and a god this will give, and that will leave,
whatever in his own heart he may wish: for he is able to do all things.”
sentences.i: and a god will give one thing and leave another, whatever he may wish in his own heart; for he can do everything.”
sentences.n: θεός without the article is 'a god' in general: no particular god is meant. τὸ μὲν ... τὸ δέ 'this ... that'. δώσει and ἐάσει are futures, 'will give' and 'will let be'. ὅττι is here ὅ τι 'whatever', not the 'because' of 441. κεν with the subjunctive ἐθέλῃ gives a general 'whatever he may wish'; ᾧ is the possessive 'his own', dative with θυμῷ 'heart', and not a relative. δύναται γὰρ ἅπαντα: δύναται is 'he is able', the god being the subject, and ἅπαντα is πάντα strengthened, 'all things together'; γάρ gives the reason for the saying. This ends Eumaeus's speech. (This unit runs past the ano teleia at the end of 444 so that the closing quotation mark and the sense stand together; the same clause stands alone in Odyssey 16.237.)

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἄργματα θῦσε θεοῖς αἰειγενέτῃσι,
σπείσας δ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον Ὀδυσσῆϊ πτολιπόρθῳ
ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔθηκεν·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai argmata thyse theois aieigenetēisi,
speisas d’ aithopa oinon Odyssēï ptoliporthōi
en cheiressin ethēken·
sentences.i: So he said, and offered the first portions to the everlasting gods, and when he had poured a libation of the wine that has the look of fire, he put it in the hands of Odysseus, sacker of cities;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί 'so he said, and' closes the speech and begins the action. ἄργματα are first pieces, the first offerings cut from the meat for the gods (from ἄρχομαι 'begin'); θῦσε is the unaugmented aorist of θύω 'offer by burning'. αἰειγενέτῃσι is a dative plural, 'ever-born' (αἰεί 'always' + γίγνομαι 'be born'). σπείσας 'having poured a libation'. αἴθοπα οἶνον 'fire-faced wine': αἴθοψ is built on αἴθω 'burn' and ὄψ 'face, look', so the wine has the look of fire. The object of ἔθηκεν, the cup, is not stated; ἐν χείρεσσιν is 'in his hands', a dative plural in -εσσι. πτολιπόρθῳ is 'sacker of cities' (πτόλις + πέρθω 'sack'), a pointed word for Odysseus, who sacked Troy.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἕζετο ᾗ παρὰ μοίρῃ.
sentences.tr: ho d’ hezeto hēi para moirēi.
sentences.l: and he sat down beside his own portion.
sentences.i: and he sat down by his own portion.
sentences.n: ὁ is the pronoun 'he', Odysseus. ἕζετο is the aorist middle of ἕζομαι 'sat down'. ᾗ is the possessive 'his own', agreeing with μοίρῃ 'portion', presumably the chine he was honoured with at 437; παρά with the dative is 'beside'.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δέ σφιν ἔνειμε Μεσαύλιος, ὅν ῥα συβώτης
αὐτὸς κτήσατο οἶος ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος,
νόσφιν δεσποίνης καὶ Λαέρταο γέροντος·
sentences.tr:
siton de sphin eneime Mesaulios, hon rha sybōtēs
autos ktēsato oios apoichomenoio anaktos,
nosphin despoinēs kai Laertao gerontos·
sentences.i: And Mesaulius shared out the food among them, a man whom the swineherd had acquired himself, on his own, while his lord was away, without his mistress or old Laertes;
sentences.n: σφιν is the dative 'to them'. ἔνειμε is the aorist of νέμω 'distribute'. Μεσαύλιος is a servant, named here with no introduction; the swineherd bought him, as the next unit says. ὅν is the relative 'whom', not the possessive. κτήσατο is the aorist middle of κτάομαι 'acquire'; αὐτὸς ... οἶος 'himself, alone'. ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος 'his lord being away' is a genitive absolute (ἀποίχομαι 'be gone'). νόσφιν 'apart from' takes the genitive: his mistress (δεσποίνης) and Laertes, γέροντος 'old'; Λαέρταο has the -αο ending. The patronymic Λαερτιάδη at 486 shows that Laertes is Odysseus's father. Line 451 is also 14.9.

sentences.t: πὰρ δ’ ἄρα μιν Ταφίων πρίατο κτεάτεσσιν ἑοῖσιν.
sentences.tr: par d’ ara min Taphiōn priato kteatessin heoisin.
sentences.l: And from the Taphians, then, him he bought with possessions his own.
sentences.i: he had bought him from the Taphians with his own possessions.
sentences.n: πάρ is παρά with its last vowel dropped; with the genitive Ταφίων it is 'from the Taphians', a people named but not described here. μιν is 'him'. πρίατο is the aorist middle of the verb 'buy', unaugmented (Attic ἐπριάμην). κτεάτεσσιν is the dative plural of κτέατα 'possessions', and ἑοῖσιν is the possessive 'his own'. The point is repeated from the last unit: the purchase was the swineherd's own.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ep’ oneiath’ hetoima prokeimena cheiras iallon.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: A set line, also 1.149: the hands go out to the food. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα, 'good things' (from ὀνίνημι 'benefit'), neuter plural; ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα is 'ready, lying set out before them'. χεῖρας is the object of ἴαλλον, imperfect of ἰάλλω 'send forth, stretch out'. οἱ δ’ is 'and they'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
σῖτον μέν σφιν ἀφεῖλε Μεσαύλιος, οἱ δ’ ἐπὶ κοῖτον
σίτου καὶ κρειῶν κεκορημένοι ἐσσεύοντο.
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
siton men sphin apheile Mesaulios, hoi d’ epi koiton
sitou kai kreiōn kekorēmenoi esseuonto.
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
the food, indeed, from them took away Mesaulius, and they to bed
of food and of meats having had their fill hastened.
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, Mesaulius took the food away from them, and they, with their fill of food and meat, hurried to their beds.
sentences.n: ἐξ ... ἕντο is tmesis for ἐξέντο, 'put away', from ἵημι; ἔρον 'desire' is its object and πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος 'for drink and food' depends on it. The line is also 1.150. σφιν is here 'from them', with ἀφεῖλε, the augmented aorist of ἀφαιρέω 'take away'. κοῖτον is 'bed'. ἐσσεύοντο is the imperfect middle of σεύω 'hurry'; the doubled σ comes from the augment. κεκορημένοι is the perfect middle participle of κορέννυμι 'satisfy', in a Homeric form (Attic κεκορεσμένοι); σίτου καὶ κρειῶν 'of food and meats' is genitive.

sentences.t:
νὺξ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπῆλθε κακὴ σκοτομήνιος, ὗε δ’ ἄρα Ζεὺς
πάννυχος, αὐτὰρ ἄη Ζέφυρος μέγας αἰὲν ἔφυδρος.
sentences.tr:
nyx d’ ar’ epēlthe kakē skotomēnios, hye d’ ara Zeus
pannychos, autar aē Zephyros megas aien ephydros.
sentences.l:
And night came on, evil, moonless, and rained, then, Zeus
all night long, and blew the West Wind, great, always wet.
sentences.i: A foul, moonless night came on, and Zeus rained all night long, while the great West Wind blew, always wet.
sentences.n: νὺξ ἐπῆλθε κακή 'a foul night came on'; σκοτομήνιος 'moonless' is built from σκότος 'darkness' and μήνη 'moon'. ὗε is the imperfect of ὕω 'rain': 'Zeus rained' is the way Homer says 'it rained', and πάννυχος 'all night long' agrees with Ζεύς. ἄη is the imperfect of ἄημι 'blow'. Ζέφυρος is the West Wind; μέγας αἰὲν ἔφυδρος 'great, always wet' (ἔφυδρος, apparently from ἐπί and ὕδωρ 'water'). The weather prepares for what Odysseus does next.

sentences.t:
τοῖς δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς μετέειπε, συβώτεω πειρητίζων,
εἴ πώς οἱ ἐκδὺς χλαῖναν πόροι, ἤ τιν’ ἑταίρων
ἄλλον ἐποτρύνειεν, ἐπεί ἑο κήδετο λίην·
sentences.tr:
tois d’ Odyseus meteeipe, sybōteō peirētizōn,
ei pōs hoi ekdys chlainan poroi, ē tin’ hetairōn
allon epotryneien, epei heo kēdeto liēn·
sentences.l:
And among them Odysseus spoke, the swineherd testing,
if somehow for him, having stripped himself, a cloak he might give, or any of the companions
another he might urge on, since of him he cared exceedingly:
sentences.i: Odysseus spoke among them, testing the swineherd, to see whether he would strip himself and give him a cloak, or urge another of the companions to, for he cared greatly for him:
sentences.n: τοῖς is the dative 'among them', with μετέειπε 'spoke among'. πειρητίζων 'testing' takes the genitive συβώτεω (-εω for -ου). εἴ πώς 'to see if somehow', the optatives πόροι and ἐποτρύνειεν giving the possible results: οἱ 'to him', ἐκδύς 'having stripped himself' (aorist participle of ἐκδύω), πόροι 'he might give' (aorist optative of πορεῖν); ἐποτρύνειεν 'he might urge on', so 'or urge another of the companions (to give one)'. ἑο is the genitive of the pronoun, 'of him', and κήδετο 'cared for' takes it. Who cares for whom is not said; most naturally Eumaeus cares for his guest, which is why a cloak might come from him. So the story that follows is a hint for a cloak.

sentences.t:
κέκλυθι νῦν, Εὔμαιε καὶ ἄλλοι πάντες ἑταῖροι,
εὐξάμενός τι ἔπος ἐρέω·
sentences.tr:
keklythi nyn, Eumaie kai alloi pantes hetairoi,
euxamenos ti epos ereō·
sentences.l:
“Hear now, Eumaeus and all the other companions,
having declared, some word I shall say;
sentences.i: “Hear me now, Eumaeus and all you other companions; having made my declaration, I shall say a word;
sentences.n: κέκλυθι is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear'; it is singular, though addressed to all, and agrees with the first-named, Εὔμαιε. εὐξάμενος, the aorist participle of εὔχομαι, has no certain sense here: 'declaring', 'vowing', 'praying' and 'boasting' are all possible. ἔπος is 'word', τι 'some', and ἐρέω is the uncontracted future 'I shall say'. Odysseus begins a long speech which runs to 506; the story inside it is told in his own voice.

sentences.t:
οἶνος γὰρ ἀνώγει
ἠλεός, ὅς τ’ ἐφέηκε πολύφρονά περ μάλ’ ἀεῖσαι
καί θ’ ἁπαλὸν γελάσαι, καί τ’ ὀρχήσασθαι ἀνῆκε,
καί τι ἔπος προέηκεν ὅ περ τ’ ἄρρητον ἄμεινον.
sentences.tr:
oinos gar anōgei
ēleos, hos t’ epheēke polyphrona per mal’ aeisai
kai th’ hapalon gelasai, kai t’ orchēsasthai anēke,
kai ti epos proeēken ho per t’ arrēton ameinon.
sentences.l:
for wine bids me,
crazy wine, which sets even the much-minded to sing aloud
and to laugh softly, and to dance rouses,
and some word sends forth which is better unsaid.
sentences.i: for wine bids me, crazy wine, which sets even a man of many counsels singing aloud and laughing softly, and rouses him to dance, and lets slip a word that were better unsaid.
sentences.n: γάρ explains why he speaks: wine bids him. ἠλεός 'crazed, foolish' describes the wine. The three verbs ἐφέηκε, ἀνῆκε and προέηκεν are gnomic aorists, saying what wine does at any time, and English uses the present. ἐφέηκε is from ἐφίημι 'set (someone) to', ἀνῆκε from ἀνίημι 'rouse, let go', προέηκεν from προίημι 'send forth'. πολύφρονα 'of the many counsels' agrees with an unstated 'man', and περ makes it 'even'. ἁπαλόν 'softly' is a neuter adjective used as an adverb. ὅ περ τ’ ἄρρητον ἄμεινον is 'which is better unsaid' (ἄρρητος = ἀ- + ῥητός).

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν τὸ πρῶτον ἀνέκραγον, οὐκ ἐπικεύσω.
sentences.tr: all’ epei oun to prōton anekragon, ouk epikeusō.
sentences.l: But since, then, at the first I cried out, I shall not conceal it.
sentences.i: But since I cried out at the start, I will not hide it.
sentences.n: τὸ πρῶτον 'at first' is adverbial. ἀνέκραγον is the second aorist of ἀνακράζω 'cry out': he has begun to speak out, and says he will not hold back. ἐπικεύσω 'I shall conceal' is a future of ἐπικεύθω (it could also be read as a short-vowel aorist subjunctive with the same force); οὐκ 'not'. ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν 'but since, then'.

sentences.t:
εἴθ’ ὣς ἡβώοιμι βίη τέ μοι ἔμπεδος εἴη,
ὡς ὅθ’ ὑπὸ Τροίην λόχον ἤγομεν ἀρτύναντες.
sentences.tr:
eith’ hōs hēbōoimi biē te moi empedos eiē,
hōs hoth’ hypo Troiēn lochon ēgomen artynantes.
sentences.l:
Would that thus I were in my prime and might for me were firm,
as when beneath Troy an ambush we led, having arranged it.
sentences.i: If only I were in my prime, and my strength firm, as when we led an ambush beneath Troy, having arranged it.
sentences.n: εἴθε begins a wish with the optative: ἡβώοιμι (from ἡβάω 'be in the prime of youth', uncontracted, Attic ἡβῷμι) and εἴη. ὣς, with the accent, is the adverb 'so, thus', and points forward to ὡς ὅτε 'as when': he wishes to be as he was at Troy. βίη 'might', ἔμπεδος 'firm', μοι 'for me'. ὑπὸ Τροίην 'beneath Troy' has the accusative of motion. λόχον ἤγομεν is 'we led an ambush': λόχος is an ambush, or the party set in it. ἀρτύναντες 'having arranged' is the aorist participle of ἀρτύνω.

sentences.t:
ἡγείσθην δ’ Ὀδυσεύς τε καὶ Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος,
τοῖσι δ’ ἅμα τρίτος ἄρχον ἐγών·
sentences.tr:
hēgeisthēn d’ Odyseus te kai Atreïdēs Menelaos,
toisi d’ hama tritos archon egōn·
sentences.l:
And led the two, Odysseus and Atreus’ son Menelaus,
and with them as third I was in command, I;
sentences.i: The two who led were Odysseus and Menelaus, son of Atreus, and with them I was the third in command;
sentences.n: ἡγείσθην is a dual verb, 'the two led', agreeing with the two named, Odysseus and Menelaus. Ἀτρεΐδης is the patronymic 'son of Atreus'. τοῖσι 'with them', ἅμα 'along', τρίτος 'as third'. ἄρχον is the imperfect of ἄρχω 'be in command'. ἐγών is ἐγώ in the form used before a vowel. The speaker puts himself beside Odysseus as a leader, in the story, and speaks to Odysseus at 484.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἄνωγον.
sentences.tr: autoi gar anōgon.
sentences.l: for they themselves bade it.
sentences.i: for they themselves bade it.
sentences.n: αὐτοί 'they themselves' is plural, continuing the two leaders of the last line. ἄνωγον is the imperfect of ἀνώγω 'bid, urge'; its object is not stated, 'that I should command'. γάρ gives the reason he was third in command.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἱκόμεσθα ποτὶ πτόλιν αἰπύ τε τεῖχος,
ἡμεῖς μὲν περὶ ἄστυ κατὰ ῥωπήϊα πυκνά,
ἂν δόνακας καὶ ἕλος, ὑπὸ τεύχεσι πεπτηῶτες
κείμεθα.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ hikomestha poti ptolin aipy te teichos,
hēmeis men peri asty kata rhōpēïa pykna,
an donakas kai helos, hypo teuchesi peptēōtes
keimetha.
sentences.l:
But when indeed we came to the city and steep wall,
we, indeed, around the town, among thick bushes,
up through reeds and marsh, under our armour having crouched
we lay.
sentences.i: But when we reached the city and its steep wall, we for our part lay crouching beneath our armour around the town, among the thick bushes, in the reeds and the marsh.
sentences.n: ἱκόμεσθα is the aorist 1 pl. of ἱκνέομαι 'come to' with the ending -μεσθα; ποτί is πρός, and πτόλιν is πόλιν. αἰπύ 'steep' agrees with τεῖχος 'wall'. ἡμεῖς μέν 'we, for our part'. ῥωπήϊα are bushes, πυκνά 'thick'. ἂν is ἀνά with its last vowel dropped, 'up through', not the particle ἄν; δόνακας 'reeds', ἕλος 'marsh'. πεπτηῶτες is the perfect participle of πτήσσω 'crouch, cower'; ὑπὸ τεύχεσι is 'under (cover of) our armour'; κείμεθα 'we lay'. The unit ends in the middle of line 475.

sentences.t:
νὺξ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπῆλθε κακὴ Βορέαο πεσόντος,
πηγυλίς·
sentences.tr:
nyx d’ ar’ epēlthe kakē Boreao pesontos,
pēgylis·
sentences.l:
And night came on, evil, the North Wind having fallen,
freezing;
sentences.i: A foul night came on, freezing, when the North Wind swooped down;
sentences.n: νὺξ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπῆλθε κακή is the phrase of 457, now continued differently. Βορέαο πεσόντος is a genitive absolute: Βορέαο is the -αο genitive of Βορέης 'the North Wind', and πεσόντος 'having fallen' is of a wind that swoops down, not one that dies away. πηγυλίς 'freezing', agreeing with νύξ, is apparently from the root of πήγνυμι 'make solid, freeze'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε χιὼν γένετ’ ἠΰτε πάχνη,
ψυχρή, καὶ σακέεσσι περιτρέφετο κρύσταλλος.
sentences.tr:
autar hyperthe chiōn genet’ ēÿte pachnē,
psychrē, kai sakeessi peritrepheto krystallos.
sentences.l:
but above, snow came to be like hoar-frost,
cold, and around the shields ice was thickening.
sentences.i: and from above snow came on like hoar-frost, cold, and ice thickened around the shields.
sentences.n: χιών 'snow'. γένετ’ is the unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι 'come to be'; ἠΰτε 'like'; πάχνη 'hoar-frost'. ψυχρή 'cold' agrees with χιών. σακέεσσι is the dative plural of σάκος 'shield'. περιτρέφετο is the imperfect middle of περιτρέφω; τρέφω can mean 'thicken, make solid', so 'was thickening around'. κρύσταλλος is 'ice'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι πάντες χλαίνας ἔχον ἠδὲ χιτῶνας,
εὗδον δ’ εὔκηλοι, σάκεσιν εἰλυμένοι ὤμους·
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi pantes chlainas echon ēde chitōnas,
heudon d’ eukēloi, sakesin eilymenoi ōmous·
sentences.l:
Then all the others had cloaks and tunics,
and slept at ease, wrapped in shields as to their shoulders;
sentences.i: Then all the others had cloaks and tunics, and slept at their ease, their shoulders covered by their shields;
sentences.n: ἔχον is the imperfect of ἔχω without augment, 'had'. χλαίνας 'cloaks', χιτῶνας 'tunics'. εὗδον 'slept'; εὔκηλοι 'at ease'. εἰλυμένοι is the perfect middle participle of εἰλύω 'wrap, cover', and ὤμους is an accusative of respect, 'as to the shoulders': they lay with their shields drawn over their shoulders. Everyone else is dressed against the cold; the next lines say why the speaker is not.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ χλαῖναν μὲν ἰὼν ἑτάροισιν ἔλειπον
ἀφραδίῃς, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐφάμην ῥιγωσέμεν ἔμπης,
ἀλλ’ ἑπόμην σάκος οἶον ἔχων καὶ ζῶμα φαεινόν.
sentences.tr:
autar egō chlainan men iōn hetaroisin eleipon
aphradiēis, epei ouk ephamēn rhigōsemen empēs,
all’ hepomēn sakos oion echōn kai zōma phaeinon.
sentences.l:
But I a cloak, indeed, going, with my companions left
through folly, since not I thought that I would shiver in any case,
but followed, a shield alone having and a shining girdle.
sentences.i: But I set out and left my cloak with my companions, through folly, since I did not think I should shiver in any case, and I followed with only my shield and my shining girdle.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγώ 'but I' opens the contrast. ἰών 'going' is the participle of εἶμι; ἔλειπον is the imperfect 'was leaving'. ἀφραδίῃς 'through folly' is a dative of cause, from ἀφραδίη (ἀ- + the root of φράζομαι 'consider'). ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί, here 'I thought'; ῥιγωσέμεν is the future infinitive of ῥιγόω 'shiver'; ἔμπης 'in any case'. ἑπόμην 'I followed' is the imperfect middle of ἕπομαι. οἶον 'alone, only' goes with σάκος 'shield'; ζῶμα is a girdle; φαεινόν 'shining'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τρίχα νυκτὸς ἔην, μετὰ δ’ ἄστρα βεβήκει,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼν Ὀδυσῆα προσηύδων ἐγγὺς ἐόντα
ἀγκῶνι νύξας·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē tricha nyktos eēn, meta d’ astra bebēkei,
kai tot’ egōn Odysēa prosēudōn engys eonta
ankōni nyxas·
sentences.i: But when the night was divided in three and the stars had passed on, I then spoke to Odysseus, who was near, nudging him with my elbow;
sentences.n: τρίχα νυκτὸς ἔην 'the night was in three parts': which point of the night is meant is not certain; ἔην is an epic form of ἦν. μετὰ δ’ ἄστρα βεβήκει has μετά in tmesis, with the pluperfect of βαίνω, and means that the stars, or the night, had moved on past them; ἄστρα can be subject or object. ἐγών is ἐγώ before a vowel. προσηύδων is the imperfect of προσαυδάω 'speak to'; ἐγγὺς ἐόντα 'who was near' agrees with Ὀδυσῆα. ἀγκῶνι is the dative of ἀγκών 'elbow'; νύξας is the aorist participle of νύσσω 'prod'.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐμμαπέως ὑπάκουσε·
sentences.tr: ho d’ ar’ emmapeōs hypakouse·
sentences.l: and he at once gave ear:
sentences.i: and he gave ear at once:
sentences.n: ὁ is the pronoun 'he', Odysseus, to whom the speaker has just spoken. ὑπάκουσε is the aorist of ὑπακούω 'give ear, listen'. ἐμμαπέως 'at once, readily' is an uncommon adverb whose derivation is not certain. The colon leads to the words the speaker said to him, in the next line.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
οὔ τοι ἔτι ζωοῖσι μετέσσομαι, ἀλλά με χεῖμα
δάμναται·
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
ou toi eti zōoisi metessomai, alla me cheima
damnatai·
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, I shall not be among the living much longer: the cold is overcoming me;
sentences.n: A speech begins inside the speech: the speaker quotes what he said to Odysseus that night, so the English gives it single quotation marks. διογενές 'Zeus-sprung', Λαερτιάδη 'son of Laertes' (a patronymic) and πολυμήχαν’ (πολυμήχανε with its last vowel elided) 'many-devising' are all vocatives. οὔ τοι ἔτι is 'no longer, I tell you'. μετέσσομαι is the future of μέτειμι 'be among', with ζωοῖσι 'the living'; the doubled σ is Homeric. δάμναται 'subdues' is a present, from δάμνημι; χεῖμα is 'wintry cold'.
sentences.mark: In the tale: he speaks to Odysseus

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔχω χλαῖναν·
sentences.tr: ou gar echō chlainan·
sentences.l: for not I have a cloak;
sentences.i: for I have no cloak;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the cold's power over him: οὐ ... χλαῖναν 'not a cloak'. ἔχω 'I have'; the picture is the one drawn at 480, where he left it with his companions.

sentences.t:
παρά μ’ ἤπαφε δαίμων
οἰοχίτων’ ἔμεναι·
sentences.tr:
para m’ ēpaphe daimōn
oiochitōn’ emenai·
sentences.l:
a power deceived me
into being tunic-alone;
sentences.i: some power misled me into going about in nothing but a tunic;
sentences.n: παρά ... ἤπαφε has παρά in tmesis as the preverb, 'astray'; ἤπαφε is the aorist of ἀπαφίσκω 'deceive'. μ’ is με. δαίμων 'a power' is a god or fate whose name is not given; it is the subject. οἰοχίτων’ is οἰοχίτωνα, agreeing with με: 'in a tunic alone' (οἶος 'alone' + χιτών 'tunic'), that is, without a cloak. ἔμεναι is the infinitive εἶναι. The speaker blames some power for his own folly.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ οὐκέτι φυκτὰ πέλονται.
sentences.tr: nyn d’ ouketi phykta pelontai.
sentences.l: but now no longer are things escapable.’
sentences.i: and now there is no escape.’
sentences.n: νῦν δέ 'but now' turns from the cause to the plain fact. φυκτά is the neuter plural of φυκτός 'that can be escaped', a verbal adjective of φεύγω; πέλονται 'are, come to be'. There is no stated subject: 'now there is no escaping'. This ends the speech inside the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα νόον σχέθε τόνδ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
οἷος κεῖνος ἔην βουλευέμεν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn, ho d’ epeita noon schethe tond’ eni thymōi,
hoios keinos eēn bouleuemen ēde machesthai·
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and he then a thought held, this one, in his heart,
such as that man was for taking counsel and for fighting;
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he then had this thought in his heart, such a man was he for counsel and for fighting;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην 'so I spoke' returns from the quoted words to the story; ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί. ὁ δ’ is Odysseus. σχέθε is the unaugmented aorist of ἔχω 'hold'; νόον ... τόνδ’ 'this thought' points ahead to what he says. οἷος κεῖνος ἔην βουλευέμεν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι is 'such was that man for counsel and for fighting': κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος, ἔην is ἦν, and the infinitives, βουλευέμεν with the -έμεν ending and μάχεσθαι, say in what he was such.

sentences.t: φθεγξάμενος δ’ ὀλίγῃ ὀπί με πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr: phthenxamenos d’ oligēi opi me pros mython eeipe·
sentences.l: and, having spoken out in a small voice, a speech to me he uttered:
sentences.i: and in a low voice he spoke to me:
sentences.n: φθεγξάμενος is the aorist participle of φθέγγομαι 'utter a sound, speak out'. ὀλίγῃ ὀπί is 'in a small voice', that is a low voice, so that no one else hears; the next line gives the reason. ὀπί is the dative of ὄψ 'voice'. πρὸς ... ἔειπε has πρός in tmesis for προσέειπε 'addressed'; with μῦθον 'speech' as its object it is 'uttered a speech to me'.

sentences.t: σίγα νῦν, μή τίς σευ Ἀχαιῶν ἄλλος ἀκούσῃ.
sentences.tr: siga nyn, mē tis seu Achaiōn allos akousēi.
sentences.l: ‘Be silent, now, lest any of the Achaeans, another, hear you.’
sentences.i: ‘Be quiet now, lest some other Achaean hear you.’
sentences.n: σίγα is the imperative of σιγάω 'be silent'. μή with the aorist subjunctive ἀκούσῃ is 'lest ... hear'. σευ is the genitive of σύ, 'you', which ἀκούω takes; Ἀχαιῶν ἄλλος is 'another of the Achaeans'. The order has to be kept quiet because they lie hidden near the enemy city.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ ἐπ’ ἀγκῶνος κεφαλὴν σχέθεν εἶπέ τε μῦθον·
sentences.tr: ē kai ep’ ankōnos kephalēn schethen eipe te mython·
sentences.l: He spoke, and upon his elbow his head he held, and uttered a speech:
sentences.i: So he said, and propped his head on his elbow, and spoke:
sentences.n: ἦ is the third person of ἠμί 'say': 'so he said', closing the last speech; ἦ καί is 'he spoke, and'. ἐπ’ ἀγκῶνος is 'on his elbow', with the genitive, and σχέθεν is σχέθε with a movable ν, 'held': he propped his head on his elbow to speak to the men. εἶπέ τε μῦθον 'and uttered a speech' announces the next words.

sentences.t: κλῦτε, φίλοι·
sentences.tr: klyte, philoi·
sentences.l: ‘Hear, friends:
sentences.i: ‘Hear me, friends;
sentences.n: κλῦτε is the aorist imperative plural of κλύω 'hear'; φίλοι is the vocative 'friends'. He now speaks to all the men round him, not to the speaker alone.
sentences.mark: In the tale: Odysseus speaks to the men

sentences.t: θεῖός μοι ἐνύπνιον ἦλθεν ὄνειρος.
sentences.tr: theios moi enypnion ēlthen oneiros.
sentences.l: divine, to me, in sleep, came a dream.
sentences.i: A divine dream came to me in my sleep.
sentences.n: θεῖος 'divine' is a dream sent by a god. μοι 'to me'. ἐνύπνιον 'in sleep' is an adverb, ὄνειρος 'dream' the subject, and ἦλθεν is 'came'.

sentences.t: λίην γὰρ νηῶν ἑκὰς ἤλθομεν·
sentences.tr: liēn gar nēōn hekas ēlthomen·
sentences.l: for exceedingly from the ships far we have come;
sentences.i: for we have come much too far from the ships;
sentences.n: λίην 'exceedingly, too (far)'. ἑκάς 'far' takes the genitive νηῶν, 'from the ships' (-ηῶν for the Attic -εῶν of ναῦς). ἤλθομεν is the aorist 'we came', here 'we have come'. γάρ gives the reason for the request that follows: they are too far from the ships.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τις εἴη
εἰπεῖν Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι, ποιμένι λαῶν,
εἰ πλέονας παρὰ ναῦφιν ἐποτρύνειε νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
alla tis eiē
eipein Atreïdēi Agamemnoni, poimeni laōn,
ei pleonas para nauphin epotryneie neesthai.
sentences.l:
but would that there were someone
to tell Atreus’ son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
whether more from the ships he might urge to come.’
sentences.i: but if only someone were there to tell Agamemnon, son of Atreus, shepherd of the people, to see whether he might urge more men to come from the ships.’
sentences.n: ἀλλά τις εἴη εἰπεῖν: εἴη is the optative of εἰμί, so 'would that someone were there to tell': a wish. Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι 'Agamemnon, son of Atreus' and ποιμένι λαῶν 'shepherd of the people', a king's title, are datives. εἰ ... ἐποτρύνειε 'whether he might urge on' is an optative, as at 460–461. πλέονας 'more (men)'. παρὰ ναῦφιν 'from beside the ships' has the ending -φιν for 'from'; νέεσθαι is an uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι 'come, go'. The inner speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δ’ ἔπειτα Θόας, Ἀνδραίμονος υἱός,
καρπαλίμως, ἀπὸ δὲ χλαῖναν θέτο φοινικόεσσαν,
βῆ δὲ θέειν ἐπὶ νῆας·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, ōrto d’ epeita Thoas, Andraimonos huios,
karpalimōs, apo de chlainan theto phoinikoessan,
bē de theein epi nēas·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and then Thoas, the son of Andraemon, sprang up speedily, put off his crimson cloak, and set out to run for the ships;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ 'so he spoke' closes the quoted speech. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι 'rouse', here 'sprang up'; Θόας is Thoas, and Ἀνδραίμονος υἱός 'son of Andraemon' says which. καρπαλίμως 'speedily'. ἀπὸ ... θέτο is tmesis for ἀπέθετο 'put off'; φοινικόεσσαν is the feminine accusative of φοινικόεις 'crimson', agreeing with χλαῖναν 'cloak'. βῆ δὲ θέειν is 'set out to run' (θέειν is the uncontracted infinitive of θέω).

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐνὶ εἵματι κείνου
κείμην ἀσπασίως, φάε δὲ χρυσόθρονος Ἠώς.
sentences.tr:
egō d’ eni heimati keinou
keimēn aspasiōs, phae de chrysothronos Ēōs.
sentences.l:
but I in that man’s garment
lay gladly, and shone golden-throned Dawn.
sentences.i: and I lay with joy in his garment, and golden-throned Dawn shone.
sentences.n: ἐνὶ is ἐν. εἵματι is the dative of εἷμα 'garment'; κείνου is ἐκείνου, 'that man's', Thoas's cloak, which he left behind. κείμην is the imperfect of κεῖμαι 'lie'; ἀσπασίως 'gladly'. φάε 'shone' is a past tense of the verb 'shine' without augment. χρυσόθρονος 'golden-throned' is the stock epithet of Dawn (Ἠώς); an old alternative derives the second part from θρόνα 'embroidered flowers'. The story ends warm, which is the point of it.

sentences.t: ὣς νῦν ἡβώοιμι βίη τέ μοι ἔμπεδος εἴη·
sentences.tr: hōs nyn hēbōoimi biē te moi empedos eiē·
sentences.l: Thus now might I be in my prime, and might for me be firm;
sentences.i: If only I were in my prime now, and my strength firm;
sentences.n: This is the wish of 468 again, without εἴθε: ὣς νῦν ἡβώοιμι 'so now might I be in my prime', with the optatives ἡβώοιμι and εἴη. The story is over, and the speaker returns from it to the present.

sentences.t:
δοίη κέν τις χλαῖναν ἐνὶ σταθμοῖσι συφορβῶν,
ἀμφότερον, φιλότητι καὶ αἰδοῖ φωτὸς ἑῆος·
sentences.tr:
doiē ken tis chlainan eni stathmoisi syphorbōn,
amphoteron, philotēti kai aidoi phōtos heēos·
sentences.l:
would give, someone, a cloak in the steadings of swineherds,
on both counts, from friendship and respect for a good man;
sentences.i: one of the swineherds in the steadings would give a cloak, from both friendship and respect for a good man;
sentences.n: δοίη κέν τις is 'someone would give': the optative with κέν is 'would'. συφορβῶν is the genitive plural of συφορβός 'swineherd'; it can go with τις ('one of the swineherds') or with σταθμοῖσι ('the swineherds' steadings'), and the sense is the same. σταθμός is a farmstead. ἀμφότερον 'both' is adverbial, 'on both counts'; φιλότητι καὶ αἰδοῖ 'from friendship and respect' are datives of cause, αἰδώς being the respect owed to a guest or suppliant. ἑῆος is the genitive of ἐΰς 'good', not the possessive; φωτὸς ἑῆος is 'of a good man'.

sentences.t: νῦν δέ μ’ ἀτιμάζουσι κακὰ χροῒ εἵματ’ ἔχοντα.
sentences.tr: nyn de m’ atimazousi kaka chroï heimat’ echonta.
sentences.l: but now me they dishonour, evil clothes on my skin wearing.”
sentences.i: but as it is they dishonour me, because I wear vile clothes on my body.”
sentences.n: νῦν δέ 'but as it is' is the contrast with the wish. μ’ is με. ἀτιμάζουσι 'they dishonour' is from ἀ-τιμή 'without honour'. κακά 'evil' agrees with εἵματα, neuter plural 'clothes', and the participle ἔχοντα 'wearing' agrees with me. χροΐ is a Homeric dative of χρώς 'skin, body'. This ends the speech that began at 462.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: The line is word for word 442: the poet again turns to Eumaeus as 'you'.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον, αἶνος μέν τοι ἀμύμων, ὃν κατέλεξας,
οὐδέ τί πω παρὰ μοῖραν ἔπος νηκερδὲς ἔειπες·
sentences.tr:
ō geron, ainos men toi amymōn, hon katelexas,
oude ti pō para moiran epos nēkerdes eeipes·
sentences.l:
“Old man, a tale indeed, you see, blameless, which you recounted,
nor yet anything beside what is fitting, a gainless word, have you said;
sentences.i: “Old man, the tale you have told is blameless, and you have not yet said anything contrary to what is fitting, any word without profit;
sentences.n: ὦ γέρον 'old man'. αἶνος is a story told with a point; the word can also mean 'praise', and here the point is plain, the cloak. ἀμύμων is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known; 'blameless' is the traditional guess. μέν τοι 'indeed, you see'. ὅν is the relative 'which'; κατέλεξας is the aorist of καταλέγω 'recount'. οὐδέ τί πω 'nor yet anything'. παρὰ μοῖραν 'contrary to what is fitting' (μοῖρα 'portion, due measure'); νηκερδές 'without profit' (νη- 'not' + κέρδος 'gain'); ἔειπες 'you said'.

sentences.t:
τῷ οὔτ’ ἐσθῆτος δευήσεαι οὔτε τευ ἄλλου,
ὧν ἐπέοιχ’ ἱκέτην ταλαπείριον ἀντιάσαντα,
νῦν·
sentences.tr:
tōi out’ esthētos deuēseai oute teu allou,
hōn epeoich’ hiketēn talapeirion antiasanta,
nyn·
sentences.i: So you will lack neither clothing nor anything else that is fitting for a suppliant so much tried to have when he meets with us, for now;
sentences.n: τῷ 'therefore' is a dative used as an adverb. δευήσεαι is the future of δεύομαι 'lack', with the genitives ἐσθῆτος 'clothing' and τευ (τινος) 'anything', ἄλλου 'else'. ὧν ἐπέοιχ’ ἱκέτην ... ἀντιάσαντα is compressed: ὧν 'of which things', ἐπέοικε 'it is fitting', ἱκέτην 'a suppliant', ταλαπείριον 'much-tried', ἀντιάσαντα the aorist participle of ἀντιάω 'meet, come upon'. Line 511 is word for word 6.193, and 510 is 6.192 with τῷ in place of οὔτ’ οὖν. The unit ends with νῦν, 'now', which the next line sets against the morning.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ ἠῶθέν γε τὰ σὰ ῥάκεα δνοπαλίξεις.
sentences.tr: atar ēōthen ge ta sa rhakea dnopalixeis.
sentences.l: but from dawn, at least, your own rags you will shake about.
sentences.i: but at dawn you will be shaking about your own rags.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ 'but'; ἠῶθεν 'from dawn' has the suffix -θεν; γε 'at least'. τὰ σὰ ῥάκεα 'your own rags', ῥάκεα being the uncontracted plural of ῥάκος. δνοπαλίξεις is the future of δνοπαλίζω 'shake about, handle roughly', a rare verb whose force here is not certain: he will be back in his rags and dragging them about. What he has tonight is for tonight only.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πολλαὶ χλαῖναι ἐπημοιβοί τε χιτῶνες
ἐνθάδε ἕννυσθαι, μία δ’ οἴη φωτὶ ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pollai chlainai epēmoiboi te chitōnes
enthade hennysthai, mia d’ oiē phōti hekastōi.
sentences.l:
for not many cloaks and tunics for changing
here to put on, but one only for each man.
sentences.i: for there are not many cloaks here, nor spare tunics, to put on; there is one only for each man.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ gives the reason for the 'now' above. πολλαί 'many' agrees with χλαῖναι 'cloaks'. ἐπημοιβοί 'for changing, in exchange' describes spare clothes; τε joins χιτῶνες 'tunics'. ἕννυσθαι 'to put on' is an infinitive of purpose. ἐνθάδε 'here' has the suffix -δε. μία δ’ οἴη is 'but one only' (a cloak, understood), φωτὶ ἑκάστῳ 'for each man'. So there is no store of spare clothes.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν ἔλθῃσιν Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός,
αὐτός τοι χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα δώσει,
πέμψει δ’ ὅππῃ σε κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει.
sentences.tr:
autar epēn elthēisin Odyssēos philos huios,
autos toi chlainan te chitōna te heimata dōsei,
pempsei d’ hoppēi se kradiē thymos te keleuei.
sentences.l:
But when there has come Odysseus’ dear son,
he himself will give you a cloak and a tunic, clothes,
and will send you wherever heart and spirit bid.”
sentences.i: But when the dear son of Odysseus has come, he himself will give you a cloak and a tunic for clothing, and will send you wherever your heart and spirit bid you.”
sentences.n: ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν, 'when', with the aorist subjunctive ἔλθῃσιν (Attic ἔλθῃ). Ὀδυσσῆος is the genitive of Ὀδυσσεύς; the son is not named in this part, only called Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός. αὐτός 'himself'; τοι 'for you'; χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα 'cloak and tunic, clothes', with εἵματα in apposition. πέμψει 'will send'; ὅππῃ is 'wherever'. κραδίη θυμός τε 'heart and spirit' takes a singular verb, κελεύει, for the two. This ends Eumaeus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἀνόρουσε, τίθει δ’ ἄρα οἱ πυρὸς ἐγγὺς
εὐνήν, ἐν δ’ ὀΐων τε καὶ αἰγῶν δέρματ’ ἔβαλλεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn anorouse, tithei d’ ara hoi pyros engys
eunēn, en d’ oïōn te kai aigōn dermat’ eballen.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he sprang up, and was setting then for him near the fire
a couch, and in it of sheep and of goats skins he was throwing.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sprang up, and made a couch for him near the fire, throwing on it the skins of sheep and goats.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών 'so having spoken'. ἀνόρουσε is the unaugmented aorist of ἀνορούω 'spring up'. τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι, 'was setting', with the dative οἱ 'for him'; πυρὸς ἐγγύς is 'near the fire'. εὐνή is a bed, here a couch of skins. ἐν δ’ ... ἔβαλλεν is tmesis for ἐνέβαλλεν 'was throwing in, on it', an imperfect of repeated action; ὀΐων τε καὶ αἰγῶν 'of sheep and of goats', δέρματ’ 'skins'.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς κατέλεκτ’·
sentences.tr: enth’ Odyseus katelekt’·
sentences.l: There Odysseus lay down;
sentences.i: There Odysseus lay down;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ 'there'. κατέλεκτ’ is κατέλεκτο, the aorist middle of καταλέγω 'lay oneself down'. It is the same verb as κατέλεξας 'recounted' at 508; in the middle it means 'lie down'.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ χλαῖναν βάλεν αὐτῷ
πυκνὴν καὶ μεγάλην, ἥ οἱ παρεκέσκετ’ ἀμοιβάς,
ἕννυσθαι ὅτε τις χειμὼν ἔκπαγλος ὄροιτο.
sentences.tr:
epi de chlainan balen autōi
pyknēn kai megalēn, hē hoi parekesket’ amoibas,
hennysthai hote tis cheimōn ekpaglos oroito.
sentences.l:
and over him a cloak he threw
thick and large, which for him used to lie by, as a change,
to put on whenever some terrifying storm might arise.
sentences.i: and he threw over him a thick, large cloak, which he kept beside him as a spare, to put on whenever some terrifying storm arose.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ ... βάλεν is tmesis for ἐπέβαλεν 'threw over'; αὐτῷ is the dative 'him', so with the verb 'threw over him'. πυκνήν 'thick' and μεγάλην 'large' agree with χλαῖναν. ἥ οἱ παρεκέσκετ’: οἱ 'for him' is Eumaeus, and παρεκέσκετ’ is an iterative past, 'used to lie by'; it was his own spare cloak. ἀμοιβάς 'as a change', ἕννυσθαι 'to put on'. ὅτε ... ὄροιτο 'whenever ... arose' is an optative in a general clause. ἔκπαγλος 'terrifying' is from ἐκπλήσσω 'strike out of one's senses'; χειμών is a wintry storm.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν ἔνθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς κοιμήσατο, τοὶ δὲ παρ’ αὐτὸν
ἄνδρες κοιμήσαντο νεηνίαι·
sentences.tr:
hōs ho men enth’ Odyseus koimēsato, toi de par’ auton
andres koimēsanto neēniai·
sentences.l:
So he, indeed, there, Odysseus, went to sleep, and they beside him
men went to sleep, young ones;
sentences.i: So Odysseus went to sleep there, and the young men went to sleep beside him;
sentences.n: ὣς ὁ μὲν ... τοὶ δέ 'so he ... but they': τοί is the pronoun 'they', and ἄνδρες νεηνίαι 'young men' is in apposition. κοιμήσατο and κοιμήσαντο are aorist middles of κοιμάω 'put to sleep', so 'went to sleep'. παρ’ αὐτόν 'beside him'. The young men are the other companions of 462. The unit ends in the middle of line 524.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ συβώτῃ
ἥνδανεν αὐτόθι κοῖτος, ὑῶν ἄπο κοιμηθῆναι,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἄρ’ ἔξω ἰὼν ὡπλίζετο·
sentences.tr:
oude sybōtēi
hēndanen autothi koitos, hyōn apo koimēthēnai,
all’ ho g’ ar’ exō iōn hōplizeto·
sentences.i: but the swineherd did not like to sleep there, away from his pigs; he went outside and armed himself;
sentences.n: ἥνδανεν is the imperfect of ἁνδάνω 'please' (Attic ἀρέσκω), with the dative συβώτῃ 'to the swineherd'; κοῖτος is 'the bed, the sleeping-place', the subject; αὐτόθι 'there'. ὑῶν ἄπο is 'away from the pigs': the preposition follows its noun and takes the accent. κοιμηθῆναι is an aorist passive infinitive with the sense 'to sleep'. ὅ γε is 'he, for his part'; ἰών 'going'. ὡπλίζετο is the imperfect middle of ὁπλίζω 'arm himself', and the next lines list what he takes.

sentences.t:
χαῖρε δ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
ὅττι ῥά οἱ βιότου περικήδετο νόσφιν ἐόντος.
sentences.tr:
chaire d’ Odysseus,
hotti rha hoi biotou perikēdeto nosphin eontos.
sentences.l:
and rejoiced Odysseus,
because, you see, of his livelihood for him he cared greatly, he being away.
sentences.i: and Odysseus was glad because he took such care of his property for him while he was away.
sentences.n: χαῖρε here is a past tense, 'rejoiced', not the greeting. ὅττι is 'because' (as at 441), and ῥά is the particle 'you see'. οἱ 'for him' is Odysseus. βιότου is the genitive of βίοτος 'livelihood, property', the object of περικήδετο 'cared greatly for' (the imperfect middle of περικήδομαι). νόσφιν ἐόντος 'while he was away' is a genitive participle that agrees with the unstated owner of βιότου, 'his' (Odysseus); it does not agree with οἱ, which is dative. The subject of the caring is the swineherd, and Odysseus is pleased by his faithfulness.

sentences.t:
πρῶτον μὲν ξίφος ὀξὺ περὶ στιβαροῖς βάλετ’ ὤμοις,
ἀμφὶ δὲ χλαῖναν ἑέσσατ’ ἀλεξάνεμον, μάλα πυκνήν,
ἂν δὲ νάκην ἕλετ’ αἰγὸς ἐϋτρεφέος μεγάλοιο,
εἵλετο δ’ ὀξὺν ἄκοντα, κυνῶν ἀλκτῆρα καὶ ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr:
prōton men xiphos oxy peri stibarois balet’ ōmois,
amphi de chlainan heessat’ alexanemon, mala pyknēn,
an de nakēn helet’ aigos eÿtrepheos megaloio,
heileto d’ oxyn akonta, kynōn alktēra kai andrōn.
sentences.l:
First, indeed, a sharp sword about his stout shoulders he slung,
and about him a cloak he put on, wind-warding, very thick,
and up a skin he took of a well-nourished goat, great,
and he took a sharp javelin, a warder-off of dogs and of men.
sentences.i: First he slung a sharp sword about his stout shoulders, and put on a very thick cloak to keep out the wind, and took up the skin of a great, well-fed goat, and took a sharp javelin, a defence against dogs and men.
sentences.n: Four things are put on or taken up, the first three with their preverbs in tmesis: περὶ ... βάλετ’ (περιβάλλομαι), ἀμφὶ ... ἑέσσατ’ (the aorist middle of ἕννυμι 'put on about himself'), ἂν ... ἕλετ’ (ἀνά again, 'took up'), and, with no preverb, εἵλετο 'took'. στιβαροῖς is 'stout'. ἀλεξάνεμον 'wind-warding' is built on ἀλέξω 'ward off' and ἄνεμος 'wind'; μάλα πυκνήν 'very thick'. νάκη is a skin or fleece; ἐϋτρεφέος 'well-nourished'. ἄκοντα 'javelin'; ἀλκτῆρα is 'one who wards off', with the genitives κυνῶν καὶ ἀνδρῶν 'dogs and men'.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι κείων ὅθι περ σύες ἀργιόδοντες
πέτρῃ ὕπο γλαφυρῇ εὗδον, Βορέω ὑπ’ ἰωγῇ.
sentences.tr:
bē d’ imenai keiōn hothi per syes argiodontes
petrēi hypo glaphyrēi heudon, Boreō hyp’ iōgēi.
sentences.l:
He set out to go, to lie down, where indeed the swine, white-toothed,
under a rock, hollow, were sleeping, in shelter from the North Wind.
sentences.i: and he set out to go and lie down where the white-toothed swine were sleeping beneath a hollow rock, in shelter from the North Wind.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι is 'he set out to go' (ἴμεναι is the infinitive of εἶμι). κείων is not the κείων of 425: it is a participle from the root of κεῖμαι 'lie', with the sense 'wishing to lie down, going to lie down'. ὅθι περ is 'just where'; σύες 'swine' and ἀργιόδοντες 'white-toothed', as at 423 and 438. πέτρῃ ὕπο γλαφυρῇ 'under a hollow rock': ὕπο follows its noun and takes the accent. εὗδον 'were sleeping'. Βορέω is a genitive of Βορέης, beside Βορέαο at 475; ἰωγή is 'shelter', so 'in shelter from the North Wind'. The part ends with Eumaeus going out to lie beside his pigs.
